title: Bath memory as a precision resource in quantum transport
authors: José Molina, Sheikh Parvez Mandal, Mahasweta Pandit, Javier Prior
abstract: Structured baths can reshape transport fluctuations in mesoscopic quantum devices, yet a predictive criterion for when this enhances precision has been lacking. We propose a route towards such precision advantages by utilizing bath memory in coherent fermionic transport through a noninteracting quantum-dot chain. Using the Landauer-Büttiker formalism, we derive a dual impedance-matching condition that synchronizes the conductor mode splitting, boundary dissipation, and bath bandwidth, and sustains constructive multimode interference across the transmission window. The analytical predictions for the optimal bath bandwidths show excellent agreement with exact nonequilibrium Green's function calculations of the transport for Lorentzian, Gaussian, and Newns spectral densities. The prescription yields an optimal bath bandwidth at which the current Fano factor is minimized and the thermodynamic and kinetic precision coefficients are simultaneously enhanced beyond their Markovian limits. The alignment of the optimal precision regime with the experimentally accessible current Fano factor minimum thus provides a practical strategy for designing precision-enhanced transport in mesoscopic platforms such as semiconductor quantum-dot arrays and ultracold fermionic channels.
summary: The paper demonstrates how incorporating finite memory into the environment (bath) of a mesoscopic conductor can act as a resource to enhance transport precision. By deriving a dual impedance-matching condition, authors predict optimal bath bandwidths that suppress current noise below Markovian limits. This offers a practical strategy for designing next-generation quantum electronic devices.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a predictive criterion for when utilizing 'bath memory' enhances quantum transport precision, addressing the lack of such a transferable connection between bath timescale and noise reduction in mesoscopic devices.
main_result: Optimal transport precision (minimum Fano factor) can be achieved by implementing a 'dual impedance-matching condition' that synchronizes internal mode splitting, boundary dissipation, and finite bath bandwidth.
method: The analysis employs the Landauer–Büttiker formalism combined with Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) techniques to calculate current noise statistics in the presence of structured baths.
model_or_system: The model is fermionic transport through a noninteracting quantum-dot chain coupled to two external fermionic baths. The bath structure is varied from Markovian wide-band limits to finite memory models using Lorentzian, Gaussian, or Newns spectral densities.
key_observables: Current Fano factor (F), thermodynamic and kinetic precision coefficients ($Q_T, Q_K$), and the transmission function $T(\omega)$.
important_parameters: Bath bandwidth ($\eta$), coupling strength ($g$), bias voltage ($eV$), and system size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on the high-bias regime ($eV \gg T$) for analytical tractability, though generalizations are made.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate Fano factor minima (a1) and optimal parameter pairs $(g, \eta)$ compared to theory; Figure 4 shows how the predicted minimum tracks across different bath spectral densities (Lorentzian, Gaussian, Newns).
paper_structure: The paper systematically derives a dual impedance-matching condition by analyzing how finite memory ($\eta$) allows for constructive interference between transport modes. This leads to an analytical scaling law that predicts optimal bandwidths matching the internal system parameters.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, tunable engineering principles—a 'design blueprint'—for enhancing quantum coherence and reducing noise in solid-state devices by controlling environmental coupling memory effects.
